paragraphs: The paper studies alignment when users have different, potentially conflicting preferences. Its setup lets a model generate several candidate responses and lets each user choose their favorite. Alignment is then measured by how often that selected response beats an answer from another model. Universal alignment means this win rate approaches one as the number of candidates grows.

The authors characterize the best general convergence rate: with k candidates, a suitable family of policies achieves a win rate of k/(k+1), and no method can improve that rate in general. They also show that a method optimal for one response, such as Nash learning from human feedback, can fail to benefit from additional samples when its outputs lack diversity.

To preserve useful diversity, they introduce symmetric multiplayer alignment games. Any symmetric Nash equilibrium of the corresponding game achieves the optimal guarantee. They also establish convergence guarantees for self-play learning and extend the framework to opponents offering multiple responses. The result makes output diversity central to the theoretical value of additional inference computation.
icml-2026-asymptotic-universal-alignment.tldr: A theoretical alignment framework shows how diverse candidate responses can achieve an optimal improvement in user-preference win rates as sampling increases.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for graph optimization often need to adapt to problems beyond those used in their initial training. This paper investigates whether known mathematical relationships between optimization problems can guide that transfer. The aim is to learn representations that remain useful across several tasks, reducing the work needed to adapt a model to another problem.

The authors first build a graph neural network encoder using a GCON module for expressive message passing and energy-based unsupervised training objectives. Trained separately, it performs competitively on multiple tasks. They then design pretraining and fine-tuning strategies informed by computational reductions, testing transfer among minimum vertex cover, maximum independent set, and maximum clique, alongside broader multitask training.

The broader setting also includes maximum cut, minimum dominating set, and graph coloring. When one task is withheld from pretraining, subsequent fine-tuning on it almost always converges faster while avoiding negative transfer in the reported setting. These findings support the viability of shared representations for graph optimization, with problem relationships providing useful guidance for training.
icml-2026-can-computational-reducibility.tldr: Pretraining informed by computational reductions helps graph optimization models transfer across tasks and usually speeds adaptation to a withheld task.

paragraphs: Protein binder design becomes more demanding when one sequence must work across several targets or several structural states. Existing generative approaches largely assume a single target in a single state, which restricts their ability to address these broader requirements. Chamaileon treats the different binding situations as contexts within a shared design problem.

Its training approach, In-Context Complex Co-Design, models protein sequence and structure together while accounting for context. This gives the framework a way to represent binding requirements across different situations. At inference time, Mixture-of-Paths Sampling optimizes a single sequence across contexts, addressing the need for a common design while alleviating the scarcity of high-quality paired data covering multiple conformations.

The authors evaluate the framework on a newly constructed benchmark called CROSS. They report that Chamaileon generates sequences adaptable to varied conformational landscapes and multiple targets. The contribution is a unified approach to requirements that single-state design handles only narrowly: the generated sequence is assessed against several binding contexts within the same modeling framework.
icml-2026-chamaileon-cross-context-binde.tldr: Chamaileon jointly models sequence and structure to design protein binders that accommodate multiple targets or structural states.

paragraphs: The paper considers recovering a sparse vector from a noisy matrix containing its outer product. Sparsity means that only s coordinates are nonzero. A central difficulty is the gap between the signal strength that theoretically contains enough information for recovery and the stronger signal required by existing polynomial-time algorithms.

The proposed column thresholding method reduces the required signal scaling from roughly s to roughly the square root of s, ignoring logarithmic factors. It achieves this for both estimating the vector and identifying its nonzero coordinates. The guarantee requires a non-uniformity condition: at least one coordinate must retain a magnitude bounded below by a constant.

That condition is essential to the scope of the result. It excludes uniform spikes, for which planted-clique-based hardness results apply, and identifies a specific class where weaker signals suffice. Starting from the thresholding estimate, the authors also develop a truncated power method with provable linear convergence. The work therefore narrows the computational-statistical gap for this structured class without claiming to resolve the unrestricted problem.
icml-2026-column-thresholding-for-sparse.tldr: Column thresholding recovers certain non-uniform sparse signals at near information-theoretic signal strength, followed by provably convergent refinement.

paragraphs: Deep Flow Networks are function approximators for discrete inputs, such as vectors of integers. Their design draws on minimum-cost flow problems, where specified imbalances at network nodes determine the cheapest feasible flow. The resulting value functions have a discrete convexity property called M-convexity, which allows efficient optimization.

The authors generalize these flow-based functions and prove a universality result: Deep Flow Networks can approximate discrete functions on integer vectors that admit convex extensions to real-valued space. They also characterize optimization complexity according to how far a network departs from the M-convex regime. This connects the model's expressive range to the mathematical structure that makes optimization manageable.

Using these theoretical results, the paper develops a practical implementation that learns from data. Experiments with different underlying functions show strong approximation accuracy and substantially faster optimization than the benchmark approaches. The contribution combines learning a useful discrete function with making that learned function efficient to optimize, while its universality guarantee applies specifically to functions possessing convex extensions.
icml-2026-deep-flow-networks-644f7cdea7.tldr: Deep Flow Networks generalize flow optimization value functions to learn expressive discrete models that remain efficient to optimize.

paragraphs: Flow matching policies produce actions through a sequence of refinement steps, offering a promising approach to offline reinforcement learning. Optimizing these policies by backpropagating through the full sequence can be unstable. Existing approaches often distill the sequence into a single-step approximation, which may reduce the benefits of iterative refinement.

Direct Flow Q-Learning introduces a surrogate objective that trains the iterative policy without backpropagation through time or distillation. It uses gradients of the terminal Q-value as guidance within each step's velocity field. This connects the value of the eventual action to the updates that construct it, while preserving the policy's multiple refinement steps.

The authors report stable optimization and state-of-the-art results across 73 tasks in OGBench and D4RL. They also apply the same framework to an offline-to-online setting, obtaining substantial gains without further modification. The stated findings suggest that directly guiding the flow's individual steps can retain its expressive capacity while avoiding the training difficulty associated with differentiating through the entire trajectory.
icml-2026-direct-flow-q-learning-e85d1b4.tldr: Direct Flow Q-Learning trains iterative flow policies with terminal value guidance, avoiding both backpropagation through time and distillation.

paragraphs: Learned image compression typically uses entropy coding to turn a latent representation into a compact bitstream. Because that coding is usually sequential, it can become a latency bottleneck. EF-LIC removes entropy coding and instead targets the statistical redundancy and dependencies inside the representation itself, supporting multiple compression rates.

The framework introduces unconstrained vector quantization, with a proof that its index distribution approaches the maximum-entropy bound and therefore leaves minimal statistical redundancy. A context-conditioned autoregressive transform reparameterizes the latents to reduce their interdependence. The theoretical analysis shows that this approach can remove correlation redundancy as effectively as conventional learned compression with entropy coding.

On Kodak, the authors report up to 67.86% bitrate reduction relative to MS-ILLM when evaluated with LPIPS. A separate ablation comparison finds compression performance matching an entropy-coded variant, alongside more than threefold faster encoding and fivefold faster decoding. These results support moving redundancy reduction into the learned representation as a way to retain compression effectiveness while reducing coding latency.
icml-2026-efficient-learned-image-compre.tldr: EF-LIC removes entropy coding by reducing redundancy in learned representations, matching its entropy-coded variant while substantially accelerating encoding and decoding.

paragraphs: A wrong factual answer can reflect either missing knowledge or a failure to retrieve knowledge already encoded in a model. This paper separates those possibilities through a behavioral framework organized around individual facts. It profiles whether a fact is encoded and whether it is inaccessible, directly recallable, or recallable only with additional inference-time thinking.

The authors introduce WikiProfile, built through an automated pipeline using a prompted language model grounded in web search. Across four million responses from 13 models, their profiling finds that GPT-5 and Gemini-3 encode 95–98% of the benchmark's facts. Despite that high coverage, failures to access encoded information remain a major source of incorrect answers.

Those recall failures disproportionately involve long-tail facts and questions asked in the reverse direction. Additional thinking recovers a substantial fraction of failures. The findings suggest that, on this benchmark, improving access to existing knowledge could provide important gains, and that factuality evaluations become more informative when they distinguish knowledge coverage from the ability to recall it.
icml-2026-empty-shelves-or-lost-keys-rec.tldr: Fact-level profiling finds that many benchmark factual errors come from failed recall of encoded knowledge, and additional thinking can recover a substantial fraction.

paragraphs: Training reasoning models with reinforcement learning often depends on a task-specific verifier that judges answers. Many tasks lack such a verifier but have expert demonstrations. RARO uses those demonstrations as its learning foundation, applying inverse reinforcement learning to develop reasoning capabilities without a task-specific verification mechanism.

The method creates an adversarial interaction between an answer-generating policy and a relativistic critic. The policy learns to imitate expert answers, while the critic tries to identify the expert answer within an expert-policy pair. Both components train jointly and continuously through reinforcement learning. The authors also identify stabilization techniques required to make this coupled learning process robust.

Against strong verifier-free baselines, RARO reports accuracy gains of 13.7% on Countdown with a 1.5B model and 8.2% on DeepMath with a 7B model. It also reports a 19.1% win-rate gain against expert poems on Poetry Writing with a 7B model. Its scaling trends resemble those of verifier-based reinforcement learning, supporting demonstrations as a useful basis for reasoning-focused training.
icml-2026-escaping-the-verifier-learning.tldr: RARO trains a policy and comparative critic from expert demonstrations, improving reasoning and poetry results without task-specific verifiers.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a spectrally sparse signal can be expressed as completing a low-rank Hankel matrix. This formulation turns signal recovery into a structured matrix problem. The paper develops a gradient descent method designed to keep each iteration inexpensive while reducing the number of iterations needed to reach an accurate reconstruction.

The method uses Jacobi preconditioning and achieves linear convergence at a rate independent of the condition number. For its analysis, the authors introduce a generator mapping factor-based iterates into matrix space. This establishes an equivalence with manifold-based methods and allows convergence to be studied directly, avoiding the need to define distances amid ambiguities in complex-symmetric factorization.

Experiments across a broad range of problem settings show fewer iterations and lower computation time than the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution brings together an efficient update rule and an analysis that handles the factorization's representational ambiguity. Its reported benefit is therefore both theoretical, through the convergence rate, and practical, through the observed reduction in reconstruction time.
icml-2026-fast-spectrally-sparse-signal-.tldr: Jacobi-preconditioned gradient descent accelerates spectrally sparse signal reconstruction with inexpensive iterations and a condition-number-independent linear convergence rate.

paragraphs: Unlearnable examples add imperceptible perturbations to training data to obstruct the extraction of useful representations. The authors find that existing examples can lose their protective effect after low-pass filtering. This indicates that their effective perturbations are concentrated mainly in high frequencies, leaving protection vulnerable when those frequencies are removed.

FUSE aims to distribute protection across the spectrum. During generator training, Random Spectral Masking removes a randomly selected contiguous frequency band, requiring the remaining bands to maintain unlearnability. Cross-Band Guidance additionally encourages consistency between high- and low-frequency components. It strengthens low-frequency protection while regulating high-frequency perturbations to preserve the image's semantic fidelity.

Experiments across multiple datasets, architectures, and spectral filtering conditions demonstrate strong protection from FUSE. The approach matters because it directly targets the frequency concentration associated with the observed failure. Its training procedures encourage different parts of the spectrum to contribute, reducing dependence on the high-frequency signals that low-pass filtering can discard in the tested settings.
icml-2026-fuse-full-spectrum-unlearnable.tldr: FUSE spreads protective image perturbations across frequency bands to address the low-pass filtering vulnerability of existing unlearnable examples.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models balance model scale and computation by using sparse expert computation. This paper identifies additional sparsity available at tensor and neuron levels during post-training and inference. It investigates how reorganizing experts and selectively dropping token-expert computation can improve the balance between accuracy and execution speed.

For post-training, the authors propose complete expert partitioning; for inference, they introduce threshold-based token-expert dropping. On Mixtral-8×7B, these techniques improve average accuracy by 1% across nine downstream benchmarks, including a 4% improvement on GSM8K. They then develop a dual-threshold approach with partial expert partitioning and reconstruction to further adjust the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Combining the post-training and inference optimizations produces a 1.19× MoE speedup and a 0.5% accuracy gain on Mixtral-8×7B. Inference-only optimization on OLMoE-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat reaches up to 1.41× MoE speedup with accuracy loss below 0.5%. The findings show that exploiting sparsity after pretraining can provide useful efficiency gains, with the reported speedups specifically applying to MoE computation.
icml-2026-mining-tensor-neuron-level-spa.tldr: Expert partitioning and threshold-based dropping exploit additional MoE sparsity to improve measured accuracy-efficiency trade-offs during post-training and inference.

paragraphs: Hierarchical 3D semantic segmentation assigns scene points labels at several levels of detail. Learning all these labels with one shared model can create conflicts between hierarchy levels. Class imbalance adds another difficulty: common categories can dominate training across the scene's multiple hierarchies, weakening the balance of the resulting segmentation.

The proposed framework separates its decoders late in the network and guides them with coarse-to-fine hierarchical consistency. This architecture aims to reduce underfitting and overfitting conflicts across levels while containing class imbalance within each individual hierarchy. It therefore allows the prediction branches to specialize while retaining guidance about how coarse and fine labels should relate.

A complementary contrastive learning method builds cluster-wise point-cloud features and supplies self-supervised information to improve segmentation under class imbalance. Experiments across multiple datasets and backbones show better balance among hierarchy levels and mitigation of class imbalance. The contribution addresses two interacting training problems through architectural separation and an additional learning signal derived from point-cloud clusters.
icml-2026-multi-label-learning-with-cont.tldr: Separate hierarchy decoders and cluster-based contrastive self-supervision improve balance across semantic levels and classes in 3D segmentation.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning adds new categories over time under restrictions on access to data. Strong pretrained vision models have made this setting increasingly effective, raising a question about what drives that performance. This paper examines how much can be explained by simple class-level statistics of an already learned representation.

The authors construct deliberately minimal reference methods using frozen CLIP features. Rather than continually updating the visual backbone, they maintain statistical estimators for each class and use those estimators for incremental inference. Across diverse benchmarks, this recovers a substantial fraction of the performance of static joint training, where classes are learned together.

The results show that competitive performance can arise without continual parameter updates in the studied setting. They identify class-level feature statistics as an important, previously underemphasized contributor to the success of approaches built on strong pretrained models. This offers a complementary interpretation of recent progress: some adaptation can be carried by accumulated statistical summaries when the frozen representation already supplies useful features.
icml-2026-on-the-power-of-statistics-in-.tldr: Simple class-level statistics of frozen pretrained features recover substantial class-incremental performance without continual parameter updates.

paragraphs: Score-based generation depends on estimating a distribution's score function from data. This paper asks whether a small estimation error is enough for Langevin dynamics to sample accurately. It focuses on errors measured in L² and, more generally, Lᵖ, examining whether these measures provide a reliable guarantee of sampling quality.

The authors show that they do not provide such a guarantee for Langevin dynamics. Even for simple high-dimensional distributions, an estimated score with arbitrarily small error can produce samples whose distribution remains far from the target in total variation distance over any polynomial time horizon. Small score error therefore need not translate into a close sampled distribution.

This contrasts with established diffusion-model guarantees under fairly mild regularity assumptions, where small L² score error permits faithful sampling within polynomial time. Because learned scores inevitably contain estimation error, the result gives a theoretical reason to favor diffusion models under these error criteria. It establishes a robustness failure for Langevin dynamics rather than asserting that every practical use of estimated scores must fail.
icml-2026-on-the-robustness-of-langevin-.tldr: Arbitrarily small score-estimation error can still leave Langevin sampling far from its target throughout polynomial time horizons.

paragraphs: Looped transformers repeatedly apply the same block, increasing computational depth without adding parameters. They can revise a full fixed-size prediction in parallel at each loop. Difficult problems may require long refinement trajectories, but learning those trajectories is challenging when training supplies only the final answer and gives no intermediate guidance.

Denoising Recursion Models address this by corrupting solutions with noise and training the model to undo that corruption across multiple recursive steps. The paper contrasts this with reversing corruption in a single training step, which creates a mismatch with iterative testing. Multiple-step training supplies a tractable curriculum of intermediate states and better matches how the model is used.

This setup also encourages forward-looking refinement rather than requiring each update to resolve the entire corruption immediately. In extensive experiments on ARC-AGI, the approach outperforms the Tiny Recursion Model. The finding supports training the refinement process itself: intermediate denoising tasks can help a shared recursive model learn the longer computational paths needed for structured solutions.
icml-2026-one-step-forward-and-k-steps-b.tldr: Denoising Recursion Models train multi-step recovery from corrupted solutions, improving iterative reasoning performance over TRM on ARC-AGI.

paragraphs: High-quality labels can require expensive human annotation or experiments. Pretrained AI models offer a potential way to reduce those costs, but their predictions do not automatically come with accuracy guarantees. This paper develops a dataset-curation method that uses such models while providing a statistical guarantee about the resulting labels.

The guarantee is probably approximately correct: with high probability, the overall labeling error is small. It applies nonasymptotically, meaning its validity does not depend on taking the dataset size toward infinity. The authors establish this under minimal assumptions on the dataset or AI model, connecting efficient automated labeling with a rigorous statement about dataset quality.

They demonstrate the methodology through language-model text annotation, pretrained vision-model image labeling, and AlphaFold-based protein folding analysis. These applications show the intended breadth of the approach across different kinds of expensive labels. The guarantee concerns aggregate labeling error with high probability; it provides a controlled basis for using model-generated labels without implying that every individual label is correct.
icml-2026-probably-approximately-correct.tldr: A dataset-curation method uses pretrained AI models while guaranteeing, with high probability, a small overall labeling error.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often accommodate devices with different hardware capacities and different data distributions. Extracting smaller sub-models enables participation, but the choice of neurons matters. The paper identifies parameter conflicts from stochastic selection under non-IID data and insufficient selection diversity from rigid rules as problems that limit training.

SpineFL divides every global-model layer into a mandatory backbone and a dynamic portion. All sub-models share the backbone to maintain generalization. Neurons in the dynamic portion are selected probabilistically according to historical activation frequency, with more frequently active neurons more likely to appear. This combines a common structural foundation with flexible device sub-models.

The activation-guided strategy aims to address parameter conflicts while retaining diversity in which neurons are selected. Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 3.28% over state-of-the-art heterogeneous federated learning methods. The findings support coordinating shared parameters and adaptive selection together, so that accommodating resource differences does not rely solely on random extraction or fixed neuron-selection rules.
icml-2026-required-spine-optional-limbs-.tldr: SpineFL combines a shared mandatory backbone with activation-guided neuron selection to improve heterogeneous federated learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian last layers offer inexpensive neural-network uncertainty estimates by applying Bayesian inference only to the final layer. This leaves uncertainty from earlier layers unaccounted for and can underestimate epistemic uncertainty. The paper aims to include variability from the full network while retaining the low inference cost of this restricted Bayesian treatment.

The method projects Neural Tangent Kernel features onto the space spanned by the last-layer features. This enriches posterior inference without abandoning the efficient last-layer representation. The authors prove that its posterior variances are at least as large as those of a standard Bayesian last layer. They also introduce uniform subsampling for both the projection matrix and posterior inference, deriving approximation bounds for each.

Evaluations cover UCI regression, contextual bandits, image classification, and out-of-distribution detection for images and tabular data. The authors report improved calibration and uncertainty estimates relative to standard Bayesian last layers and competitive baselines while reducing computational cost. The larger-variance guarantee addresses the identified underestimation tendency, with the empirical tests supporting the usefulness of the resulting uncertainty estimates.
icml-2026-richer-bayesian-last-layers-wi.tldr: Projected and subsampled NTK features enrich Bayesian last-layer uncertainty estimates while preserving inexpensive inference.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly filling positions in a masked sequence. Decoding therefore involves deciding both what to generate and which positions to commit next. A greedy strategy selects the most confident positions, but those local decisions can lock the model into an unfavorable unmasking order, particularly on reasoning-heavy prompts.

SOAR changes its decoding behavior according to confidence without additional training. When confidence is low, it briefly explores alternative unmasking decisions through a wider search. When confidence is high, it narrows the search and fills many positions in parallel. The two modes allocate computation differently according to the model's current uncertainty.

The authors evaluate SOAR on GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval using Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B. They report better generation quality while maintaining competitive inference speed. The findings support treating unmasking order as a meaningful search decision and using confidence to balance that search against parallel decoding, rather than applying the same amount of exploration at every denoising step.
icml-2026-search-or-accelerate-confidenc.tldr: SOAR uses confidence to alternate between exploring unmasking orders and fast parallel decoding in diffusion language models.

paragraphs: Scientific agents incur costs through their tools as well as their language-model tokens. SimulCost evaluates this issue for parameter tuning in physics simulations, comparing language models with traditional scanning on both accuracy and computational cost. Its cost definitions are analytical and platform-independent across 11 simulators covering fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and plasma physics.

The benchmark includes 2,643 single-round initial-guess tasks and 2,304 multi-round trial-and-error tasks. A twelfth production plasma simulator is reported separately because its cost is measured by wall-clock time. Frontier models achieve 45–62% success in single-round mode, falling to 34–50% when accuracy requirements are high.

Multiple rounds increase success to 66–81%, but the language-model approaches are 1.5–2.7× slower than scanning in the reported evaluations. This exposes a trade-off that success rates alone obscure: more attempts improve outcomes while increasing simulation cost. The toolkit also supports investigating parameter correlations, in-context examples, and reasoning effort, providing a basis for developing agents whose decisions account for the cost of experimentation.
icml-2026-simulcost-a-cost-aware-benchma.tldr: SimulCost finds that repeated LLM-guided physics tuning improves success but costs more computation than traditional scanning in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Vision transformer attention lacks an explicit spatial bias because of its permutation-equivariant structure. This matters especially when a model is small or training data is limited. VIOLIN introduces spatial structure directly into attention using space-filling curves, aiming to make location information easier for these models to use.

The method scans an image along multiple curves and constructs a decay mask for each one. It combines these masks and multiplies the result with the attention matrix. This changes attention according to the spatial scanning patterns while adding less than 0.0015% extra parameters and negligible computational overhead. It can also be combined with parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA.

Across VTAB-1K task groups, VIOLIN improves accuracy, with gains up to 8.7% on tasks where spatial information is essential. It also improves small ViT architectures during ImageNet-1K pretraining and delivers gains up to 7.2% in pixel-level CIFAR-100 training. The results support lightweight spatial guidance as a useful addition when model capacity or available training data is constrained.
icml-2026-spatial-priors-via-space-filli.tldr: VIOLIN injects spatial structure into vision-transformer attention using space-filling curves with negligible computational overhead.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning is often understood through attraction between matching examples and dispersion across the embedding space. This paper develops a population-level geometric account of InfoNCE. It treats representations as measures evolving on a fixed embedding manifold and connects the stochastic objective to deterministic energy landscapes in the large-batch limit.

The authors prove consistency of both objective values and gradients, then identify different behavior in unimodal and symmetric multimodal settings. For the unimodal case, the intrinsic energy is strictly convex with a unique Gibbs equilibrium; entropy selects within the aligned basin. For the multimodal case, the distributions of the two modalities reshape one another's effective landscapes through cross-coupled geometry.

A persistent negative symmetric divergence term allows strong pairwise alignment to coexist with a gap between the modalities' overall distributions. Controlled synthetic experiments and analyses of pretrained CLIP representations support these predictions. The implication is that matching individual pairs well does not by itself control population-level cross-modal structure, so alignment and distributional agreement need separate analytical attention.
icml-2026-the-geometric-mechanics-of-con.tldr: A geometric analysis of InfoNCE explains how strong pairwise alignment can coexist with persistent differences between modality distributions.

paragraphs: Generating several 3D objects from an image requires preserving both individual shapes and their relative placement. Existing approaches fine-tune image-to-3D models on multi-instance data, adding training overhead while still struggling with spatial fidelity. TIMI builds on the observation that pretrained models already contain meaningful spatial priors that remain underused.

The framework first applies Instance-aware Separation Guidance during early denoising to help disentangle objects that might otherwise become entangled. It then uses a Spatial-stabilized Geometry-adaptive Update to stabilize that guidance. This second component promotes preservation of each object's geometric characteristics while maintaining the relationships among objects in the scene.

Experiments show better global layouts and more distinct local instances than existing multi-instance methods, along with faster inference and no additional training. The contribution is a way to guide an existing generator's spatial capabilities during generation. Its two components address the linked needs to separate objects and preserve coherent geometry, making use of spatial information already present in the pretrained model.
icml-2026-timi-training-free-image-to-3d.tldr: TIMI guides pretrained image-to-3D models to separate objects and preserve their layout without additional training.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models have made progress in tasks such as captioning, segmentation, and visual grounding, but their understanding of perceptual image features remains limited. This paper focuses on aesthetics, quality, structure, and texture. It introduces UniPercept-Bench to organize and evaluate those aspects of image understanding within a common framework.

The authors establish a hierarchical definition system and construct large-scale datasets for evaluation. They then train UniPercept through domain-adaptive pretraining and task-aligned reinforcement learning. The resulting model is designed to generalize across both visual rating, which assigns assessments to images, and visual question answering, which responds to questions about them.

The paper reports that UniPercept outperforms existing multimodal language models on perceptual-level image understanding. It can also serve as a plug-and-play reward model for text-to-image generation. Together, the benchmark and model connect explicit definitions of perceptual attributes with their evaluation and learning, while extending the resulting assessments to a role in guiding image generation.
icml-2026-unipercept-towards-unified-per.tldr: UniPercept combines a perceptual image benchmark with a trained model for visual ratings, question answering, and image-generation rewards.
